Key Findings

Math Tycoon is a practice engine.
Its outcomes depend on how much calibrated practice each student gets, which in turn depends on attendance, on whether the class runs as designed, and on whether the game keeps students engaged. Those links come first in measurement.
Lando already collects the hardest data to get.
A full, student-level event history since launch records accuracy, worksheets and standards unlocked. What it does not yet show is how classes run, how students feel about math, or how they do on an achievement measure outside the app.
Published research backs the practice more than the motivation loop.
Adaptive practice and timed fact practice have rigorous support, though at higher doses than Math Tycoon delivers. The idea that themes build interest, and interest drives practice, is the least supported link, so this report treats its direction as a question to test.
Measure implementation now, outcomes next, a trial later.
Linking dose, fidelity and adult support to outcomes this year shows what Math Tycoon produces at its actual dose, and how large a later outcome study would need to be.

About Lando

Lando runs after-school enrichment classes on K–5 school campuses in California, Washington and Colorado: robotics, coding, clay, piano and math. Lando hires and trains the instructors and rents the classroom; parents pay for most classes, and some schools or PTAs fund them. This assessment covers Math Tycoon, the math class piloted in spring 2026 and launched this fall. It does not cover Lando's other subjects or its at-home AI fluency product.

The Impact Process Model

The figure below maps how Math Tycoon is intended to produce impact: from what Lando teachers deliver and what the app provides, through what students and families do and what changes in students, to outcomes, within the context of a weekly after-school class. Solid boxes mark elements that data or direct observation show are happening. Dashed boxes mark elements Lando describes but has not yet shown with data, including well-defined elements that are not yet measured. Numbered markers point to the open questions listed beneath the figure.

ℹ️ Click any column for model detail and its open question. Switch on the measurement layer to see where each priority (P1–P4) applies, and click a badge for detail.

Model Description

ElementDescription
ContextAfter school, once a week, on school campuses. A semester has 14 sessions, though schools run 4–14, in one- or two-hour classes. Classes mix grades, are taught by Lando teachers who often rotate, are mostly parent-paid and self-selected, and supplement the math students learn in school.
Lando Teachers DeliverTeachers are trained to run the class through phone-based professional development and a required math refresher test, which many teachers found hard. They are meant to run the game as designed: introduce the mechanics, score two or three open responses per student, and keep the co-op and VIP goals moving. How consistently they do so is not yet measured, so that box is dashed.
What the App ProvidesAdaptive worksheets and Bubble Pop: students start a grade below, and two stretch items per worksheet set the next one, targeting 75–85% accuracy. A themed co-op park, where worksheets earn shared revenue and build the helipad that unlocks a VIP math mini-game. A parent report card after each class with accuracy, skills to practice and a VIP selfie, opened and shared at rates near Lando's LEGO class.
What Students and Families DoStudents practice at their learning edge in high volume, which the logs show (up to about 20 worksheets or 700 correct Bubble Pops in a class). They work toward a shared class goal, nudging classmates to finish worksheets so the VIP arrives. Families are meant to practice the skills the report flags; home practice is not tracked.
What Changes in StudentsFluency and accuracy on skills students are already learning in school; math that feels relevant, social and fun, so interest grows; and gaps reinforced at home as parents target the skills the report flags. None of these is measured yet.
OutcomesNear term, mastery of more grade-level standards, tracked in the app. Math confidence and interest, Flora's guiding aim, not yet measured. Longer term, higher school math achievement on district and state tests. There is no outcome evidence yet.
Causal chainThe model is a loop rather than a line: math feels relevant, which builds interest, more practice, accuracy, confidence and then more interest. Practice drives every outcome, and motivation drives practice. Early churn would signal that the loop is broken. The direction of the loop has not been tested.

Evidence Landscape

Before identifying measurement opportunities, it is worth cataloging the evidence Lando already has. This inventory is what lets the measurement priorities read as gap-filling rather than as starting from zero.

Evidence AssetWhat It ShowsLimitations
Mixpanel event historySourceLando product analytics, mid-August 2026 onward
 Per-student accuracy over time, worksheets completed, standards unlocked, the teacher for each class, and Bubble Pop accuracy and volume. Kept as a full event history, so growth and calibration can be analyzed without new engineering. About two months of data. Teacher-scored open responses add some noise. In-app measures typically show larger gains than school tests.
Practice volumeSourceMixpanel; Felix Hu and Flora Troy
 Roughly 70–80 questions per two-hour class; some students complete about 20 worksheets in a class, and one logged 700 correct Bubble Pops. Shows how much practice happens, not what it produces. High Bubble Pop counts can include rapid guessing.
Parent report engagementSourceLando analytics
 Parents open and share the after-class report at rates close to Lando's LEGO robotics class. Parents leave fewer reviews for math than for other classes. Whether families practice at home is not tracked.
Class audio transcriptsSourceRecordings on the teacher iPad
 A record of what is said in each class, which Lando has begun querying for signs of enjoyment. Not attributed to individual speakers.
Teacher math refresher testSourceLando teacher training
 A 30-item check of grade 4–5 math required of every Math Tycoon teacher, showing where teachers need a refresher. Not yet analyzed or linked to how a teacher's classes go.
Spring 2026 pilotSourceTwo pilot schools
 Students from the pilot class re-enrolled for the same class this fall. Anecdotal, from an earlier version of the game.
Parent reviewsSourcefindlando.com
 4.97 out of 5 across more than 5,000 reviews in 108 districts. Mostly robotics, coding and clay; not specific to Math Tycoon.

Lando's strongest asset is rare at this stage: a student-level record of practice, accuracy and standards progress, kept as a full history from launch. It would be valuable to add a measure of how classes are run, a measure of how students feel about math, additional signals about parent reinforcement of skills outside of class, and a measure of achievement outside the app. The priorities below fill those gaps, starting with what the existing data can already answer.

Cobalt also reviewed the published research behind each element of the model. That review is summarized in the evidence review appendix.

Measurement Opportunities

Because Math Tycoon is a once-weekly practice program, its effect on school test scores is likely to be modest and to depend heavily on how much a student attends and how well the class runs. That makes dose and fidelity key indicators to measure, which will lay the foundation for a correlational study.

We organize the assessment into four priorities, ordered by dependency. Priorities 1–3 measure implementation: how much each student practices, whether the game runs as designed, and what the adults around the student do. Most of this can start this semester from existing logs, with small additions. Priority 4 adds outcome measures and links them to the first three, which is the correlational study.

Together they answer the questions schools and parents will ask — how well is it being used, does it work, for whom, and at what dose — in an order that builds the evidence a later outcome study needs.

The Four Priorities in Detail

Measurement Focus Which audience each priority serves Lando team Schools Parents Future study
● Primary driver    ○ Contributing factor    – Not applicable
1 Dose and Adherence — How Much Math Tycoon Each Student Gets Fall 2026 ● ○ ○ ● ▼
Start Here

In a key meta-analysis of after-school and summer programs for at-risk students, only math programs with more than 45 total hours showed a significant impact on achievement. A full 14-session semester of one- or two-hour classes amounts to 14–28 hours. That makes dose the first thing to measure.

The key task is coming up with an operational definition of dose, identifying a manageable number of metrics that reflect it, and organizing the data to facilitate product improvement and analyses examining correlations with outcomes.

Much of this is already in Mixpanel and may already be completed.

Candidates for what to measure

  • Sessions attended and total hours of class per student, accounting for one- and two-hour classes and the number of sessions each school runs
  • Worksheets and items completed per session and across the semester
  • Early churn: which students stop after the first few sessions, and how their first sessions differed from those of students who stayed
  • Re-enrollment from one semester to the next
2 Gameplay Fidelity — Whether the Game Runs as Designed Winter 2027 ● ○ – ● ▼
Start Now

Gameplay incorporates two measurable mechanisms of action. First, an adaptive engine that delivers worksheets within each child’s zone of proximal development, operationalized as a difficulty level that results in approximately 80% of items answered correctly. Second, students earn game “unlocks” when the whole class achieves completion milestones, reflecting a model of interdependence.

What to measure

  • Share of each student's worksheets with accuracy between 75% and 85%, by grade and across sessions
  • Whether each class reaches the VIP, and how long it takes
  • Each student's contribution to the class goal, to see who carries the class and who is left out

Per-student contribution also answers a design question the evidence raises. Cooperative designs show larger effects when group rewards depend on each member's learning rather than on completed work, and a shared goal can put pressure on younger or slower students in a mixed-grade room. Logging contribution lets Lando see both.

3 Adult Support — What Teachers and Parents Do Winter–spring 2027 ● ○ ● ○ ▼
Light Lift

Teacher implementation can influence gameplay and potentially impact, including how they introduce the mechanics, score open responses, and keep the class moving toward the VIP. This is particularly important because the first class, before students understand the reward structure, can be challenging. Published research on after-school math also points to staffing and format as moderators of effect, so fidelity is worth measuring from the start. However, teacher implementation is currently unmeasured, reflecting a measurement opportunity.

In addition to teachers, parents play a role in Math Tycoon’s efficacy. Parents receive a report after every class suggesting math skills a student needs to work on. The platform records open rates, which may serve as a proxy for parent involvement in supporting math. Better would be direct in-app evidence that parents affirmatively supported the math skill in question.

What to measure

  • Teacher language introducing game play (from ambient recordings), judged against a rubric describing strong implementation
  • Teacher actions logged in the app, such as time to score open responses, by teacher and session
  • Refresher-test scores and training completion per teacher, linked to fidelity and student practice in that teacher's classes
  • Parent engagement beyond opens: click-through to the suggested practice and time spent on the report
  • A one-question parent check-in every few weeks on whether the family practiced at home

Messages to parents change behavior most when they are specific about what to work on. Framing home activities as games rather than homework help keeps them low-stakes, which matters because prompting help from math-anxious parents can backfire.

4 Outcomes — What Changes in Students, Linked to Priorities 1–3 Spring 2027 ○ ● ● ● ▼
Highest Value

The Lando team has identified three measurable intended outcomes: fun, confidence and math competence. Developing usable indicators of each is foundational to linking these outcomes to dose, fidelity and adult support. That kind of correlational study shows whether students who get more of Math Tycoon, in classes run as designed, improve more, and it estimates how large the effect is.

What to measure

  • Grade-level standards mastered in the app (already operationalized)
  • Enjoyment and math confidence: one or two items at sessions 1, 5 and 10
  • Voluntary Bubble Pop play, as a behavioral sign of enjoying math
  • Fall and spring district interim math scores for participating students, under a data-sharing agreement
  • Analyses of the relationship between Priorities 1–3 and these outcomes, and the effect size it implies

What Changes If You Do This

Today Lando can show how much a child practiced and how accurately. With these four priorities in place, Lando could tell a principal how many hours of Math Tycoon it takes before district interim scores move, and whether that holds for younger students and for those who start below grade level. It could tell a parent whether their child enjoys the class and feels more confident in math, measured rather than inferred from reviews. It could tell its own team which classes run the game as designed, which teachers need support, and whether the shared park goal lifts every student or a few. And it would know, before committing to an outcome study, how large an effect to expect and how many students that study needs.

Recommended Next Steps

The first steps use data Lando already collects. The later ones need new instruments and agreements with districts.

This semester

1
Define the dose measure. Agree on how to count sessions and hours per student, and compute it from Mixpanel for fall 2026 classes (Priority 1).
2
Run the churn and calibration checks. Use existing logs to find where students drop off and whether accuracy stays in the 75–85% band (Priorities 1 and 2).
3
Add fidelity and contribution logging. Log VIP arrival, each student's contribution to the class goal and open-response scoring time, ideally in the winter release (Priorities 2 and 3).
4
Draft and pilot the affect check. Write one or two age-appropriate items on enjoyment and confidence and try them in a few classes before spring (Priority 4).

Spring 2027 and beyond

1
Secure district data. Open data-sharing conversations, with FERPA-compliant agreements, with two or three districts for fall and spring interim math scores (Priority 4).
2
Run the correlational study. Link dose, fidelity and adult support to outcomes across the spring semester, and have it reviewed against ESSA Tier III standards (Priorities 1–4).
3
Plan the causal impact study. Use the effect-size estimate to set the sample and timing of a quasi-experimental or randomized study, likely in 2027–28.

About This Report

This report has two purposes: first, to articulate a working model of the mechanisms through which Math Tycoon is intended to produce impact; and second, to identify where measurement would most improve Lando's ability to understand and demonstrate that impact. It is an assessment, not an evaluation.

  1. Articulate a working model of how Math Tycoon is intended to produce impact — from the class through student practice to outcomes.
  2. Use that model to identify and prioritize opportunities for impact measurement.

Our aim is to give Lando a sequenced plan that uses the data it already collects to show how much Math Tycoon each student gets, whether classes run as designed, and what changes in students' math and in how they feel about math, so that any later outcome study is sized and designed on evidence. Where sources disagree on program length, this report follows Lando's description of a 14-session semester.
